summary: The note explains humus, the dark, amorphous organic matter in soil formed by decomposition of plant and animal matter, and describes how it forms through humification, how stable it is, and how it benefits soil. It covers humus's nutrient content and C:N ratio, its role in moisture retention, cation exchange, buffering and drought resistance, and its possible contribution to carbon sequestration. It also notes that humus is hard to define and analyze and that the idea of stable humic substances is now debated.
one_line: Overview of humus, the dark amorphous organic matter in soil, covering its formation by humification, stability, horizons, and benefits for soil fertility.
key_facts: In classical soil science, humus is the dark organic matter in soil formed by the decomposition of plant and animal matter.
Humus is the Latin word for "earth" or "ground".
The carbon to nitrogen (C:N) ratio of humus commonly ranges between 8:1 and 15:1, with the median being about 12:1.
Fully humified humus has a uniformly dark, spongy, and jelly-like appearance and is amorphous.
Much of the humus in most soils has persisted for more than 100 years and can be regarded as stable.
Most humus that is not protected within soil aggregates or bound to clays is decomposed within 10 years.

A very stable form of humus is thought to have formed from slow oxidation of soil carbon after finely powdered charcoal was incorporated into the topsoil, speculated to be important in the formation of the Amazonian terra preta do Indio.
Humus can hold the equivalent of 80–90% of its weight in moisture.
Humus is a colloidal substance that increases the cation-exchange capacity of soil.
Lignin, quickly transformed by white-rot fungi, is one of the primary precursors of humus.
Microorganisms decompose soil organic matter into inorganic minerals in a process termed "mineralization"; a fraction that does not mineralize undergoes "humification".
Some judge earthworm humus (vermicompost) to be the optimal organic manure.
Most soils have three major horizons: the surface horizon (A), the subsoil (B), and the substratum (C).
There is now a consensus that humus functions hormonally rather than simply nutritionally in plant physiology.
Humus has a dark color that helps warm cold soils in spring.
